demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette:
Ravi is a 34-year-old delivery driver who lives with his wife in a suburban neighborhood outside of Chicago. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, after months of growing distance between them, and after a near-miss on the highway last week sent him into a shaking, tearful episode that left him pulled over on the shoulder for nearly an hour. He is a slender man with tired eyes and a careful, deliberate way of speaking, as though he is constantly weighing whether what he is about to say is safe.

The event that changed everything happened eleven months ago, on a rainy Tuesday afternoon in late October. Ravi was making his final run of the day, a bulky furniture delivery to a house on a narrow, winding road. The GPS had routed him down a street he did not know well, and the rain had made the pavement slick, the leaves on the road treacherous. As he rounded a curve, a child on a bicycle shot out from a driveway directly into his path. Ravi slammed the brakes, but the van skidded. He felt the thud before he fully understood what had happened. The boy, eight years old, was rushed to the hospital with a fractured pelvis and internal injuries. He survived, but he spent three weeks in the ICU and will walk with a limp for the rest of his life. Ravi was not charged; the police report cited the boy’s sudden entry into the road, the weather, the impossibility of stopping in time. But that official finding has never mattered to Ravi. What matters is what he replays every single night: the fraction of a second where he might have swerved harder, or honked sooner, or simply not taken that route at all.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi could not stop thinking about the moment before the impact. He became certain that he had seen a flash of movement—the boy’s yellow raincoat—a full second before he hit the brakes. He told himself that a better driver, a more alert person, would have processed that flash and reacted. He had failed to protect that child. He had been behind the wheel, and he had not done enough. The guilt settled into him like a stone. He told his wife, “I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop it.” She tried to reassure him, but her words felt hollow, even insulting, because she had not been there. She did not understand that the event happened because of the way he acted—because he had been distracted, because he had not braked hard enough, because he had not seen the boy sooner. He could not accept any other explanation.

The driving became unbearable. Every time Ravi got behind the wheel, his heart would pound and his palms would sweat. He began taking longer, safer routes to avoid curves, hills, and residential streets. His delivery times suffered, and his dispatcher started calling him about delays. He started checking his mirrors obsessively, scanning for children, for bicycles, for anything that might dart into his path. He would arrive home exhausted, his shoulders knotted, unable to speak. His wife tried to draw him out, but he felt that she could not possibly understand the weight he carried. The more she pushed, the more he withdrew. He stopped joining her for weekend errands, claiming he needed to rest. He stopped visiting his own parents, who lived forty minutes away, because the drive felt unbearable. His world shrank to the route between his home and the delivery depot, and even that was a daily trial.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was not the driving, but the marriage. Last week, his wife told him gently that she felt like she was living with a stranger, that she missed him, that she could not keep watching him suffer alone. That night, he sat on the edge of their bed and told her, for the first time, what he really believed: that he was a danger to others, that he should never have been trusted behind a wheel, that the accident proved something terrible about who he was. She held him and said, “That’s not true.” He wanted to believe her. He is here now, in this office, because he is afraid that if he does not change, he will lose her. But what he is most afraid of is this: that no amount of talking will undo what he did, and that he will carry the weight of that moment for the rest of his life.
